question: Compare PostgreSQL 17 and PostgreSQL 18 using official release notes: which performance, developer and operational features changed, and what should a small SaaS team verify before upgrading?
title: PostgreSQL 17 vs. PostgreSQL 18: Feature Comparison and SaaS Upgrade Considerations

sentences.text: PostgreSQL 17 introduced incremental backups, JSON to relational table transformations, and query optimizations for CTEs and UNION queries.
PostgreSQL 18 introduces asynchronous input/output capabilities, native UUIDv7 support via the uuidv7() function, and requires matching checksum configurations during pg_upgrade.
According to single sources, SaaS teams preparing for PostgreSQL 18 must verify extension compatibility, adjust to deprecated MD5 authentication, and account for default data checksums.
1 sentence(s) removed for insufficient evidence - see gate_result.json
PostgreSQL 17 added support for incremental backups to capture only changes made since the prior backup, as well as query optimizations leveraging statistics for CTEs and UNION queries.
PostgreSQL 17 introduced functionality to transform JSON data into relational tables within SQL environments.
According to single sources, PostgreSQL 17 reduced VACUUM memory consumption by up to 20x and achieved up to 2x better write throughput in high concurrency workloads.
PostgreSQL 18 introduces asynchronous input/output capabilities across operations such as sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, and vacuum.
PostgreSQL 18 introduces native support for UUIDv7 via the uuidv7() function.
According to single sources, PostgreSQL 18 enables data checksums by default in initdb and deprecates MD5 password authentication in favor of SCRAM-SHA-256.
When upgrading with pg_upgrade in PostgreSQL 18, data checksum settings must match between the source and target clusters.

While PostgreSQL 17 focused on incremental backups, JSON transformations, and query execution optimizations, PostgreSQL 18 expands foundational performance through asynchronous I/O, UUIDv7, and stricter security and integrity defaults.

k1.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduces support for incremental backups, which captures only the changes made since the last backup rather than a full database copy.

k2.statement: PostgreSQL 17 includes functionality to transform JSON data into relational tables, simplifying JSON processing within SQL environments.

k3.statement: PostgreSQL 17 improves query performance for Common Table Expressions (CTEs) and UNION queries by leveraging statistics from earlier parts of the query in the execution plan.

k4.statement: PostgreSQL 17 includes a new internal memory structure for the vacuum process that consumes up to 20x less memory.

k5.statement: High concurrency workloads in PostgreSQL 17 may see up to 2x better write throughput due to improvements with write-ahead log (WAL) processing.

k6.statement: PostgreSQL 17 adds AVX-512 SIMD support for the bit_count function.

k7.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduces the JSON_TABLE command to convert JSON data into a standard PostgreSQL table.

k8.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduced a built-in, immutable collation provider that uses UTF-8 encoding.

k9.statement: Upgrades from PostgreSQL 17 allow users to retain logical replication slots, avoiding the need to re-synchronize data.

k10.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduces the pg_createsubscriber tool to speed up the initial data copy process for logical replication.

k11.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduced a new memory management system for VACUUM that reduces memory consumption and improves vacuuming performance.

k12.statement: The COPY command in PostgreSQL 17 includes a new option, ON_ERROR ignore, allowing operations to continue despite errors.

k13.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduced pg_createsubscriber, a utility to create logical replicas from physical standbys.

k14.statement: PostgreSQL 17 added support for incremental backups via pg_basebackup.

k15.statement: PostgreSQL 17 provides query performance improvements for sequential reads using streaming I/O and write throughput under high concurrency.

k16.statement: PostgreSQL 17 overhauled vacuum memory management, reducing memory usage by up to 20x.

k17.statement: PostgreSQL 17 supports up to 2x higher write throughput for high-concurrency workloads due to WAL improvements.

k18.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduced the JSON_TABLE function to transform JSON data into relational tables on the fly.

k19.statement: PostgreSQL 17 added logical replication failover support, allowing replication to continue automatically during primary failover.

k20.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduced the pg_maintain role and MAINTAIN privilege to allow non-superusers to perform maintenance tasks.

k21.statement: Preserved logical replication slots in PostgreSQL 17 allow logical replicas to remain connected during future major version upgrades including 17 to 18.

k22.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces skip scans for multi-column indexes, allowing indexes to be used even when the query does not filter on the first column.

k23.statement: Generated columns in PostgreSQL 18 default to virtual, meaning they are calculated on read rather than stored on disk.

k25.statement: New PostgreSQL 18 clusters enable page checksums by default.

k27.statement: The MD5 password authentication method is deprecated in PostgreSQL 18.

k29.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces native support for UUIDv7 via the uuidv7() function.

k30.statement: MD5 password authentication is deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 in favor of SCRAM-SHA-256 and is planned for removal in the next major release.

k31.statement: PostgreSQL 18 requires either a dump/restore or pg_upgrade for migration from earlier versions.

k32.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces an asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem, supporting sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, and vacuum, which can improve throughput by issuing multiple concurrent I/O requests.

k33.statement: PostgreSQL 18 enables planner statistics to be retained through a major version upgrade, preventing query performance degradation on busy systems.

k35.statement: Databases initialized with initdb in PostgreSQL 18 have page checksums enabled by default, which requires specifying --no-data-checksums when using pg_upgrade for clusters without them.

k36.statement: Major upgrades of PostgreSQL require a dump/reload of the database or the use of the pg_upgrade application because data directory contents cannot be maintained in a backward compatible way.

k37.statement: Minor release upgrades in PostgreSQL are performed by stopping the database server, installing updated binaries, and restarting the server, without needing a dump and restore.

k38.statement: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group supports a major version for 5 years after its initial release.

k39.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces an asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem to improve performance for operations like sequential scans, bitmap heap scans, and vacuums.

k40.statement: PostgreSQL 18 changes the default behavior of initdb to enable data checksums.

k41.statement: The pg_upgrade tool in PostgreSQL 18 now retains optimizer statistics.

k42.statement: PostgreSQL 18 disallows the use of the `\.` sequence as an end-of-file marker when reading CSV files via COPY FROM.

k43.statement: initdb defaults to enabling data checksums in PostgreSQL 18; pg_upgrade requires matching checksum settings between the old and new cluster.

k44.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces an Asynchronous I/O (AIO) subsystem to improve read-heavy scan performance and reduce maintenance I/O slowdowns.

k45.statement: PostgreSQL 18 enables data checksums by default for new clusters initialized with initdb.

k46.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces support for OAuth authentication.

k47.statement: Data checksum settings must match between the source and target clusters when using pg_upgrade in PostgreSQL 18.

k48.statement: SaaS teams must verify that all database extensions, such as pgvector or PostGIS, are compatible with PostgreSQL 18 before upgrading.

k50.statement: The psql client now supports a pipeline mode, allowing multiple SQL commands to be sent without waiting for each to complete.

k51.statement: PostgreSQL 18 adds a --swap option to pg_upgrade, which moves data directories instead of copying files to improve transfer speed.

k52.statement: For backward compatibility in pg_dump, basic statistics are not dumped by default.

k53.statement: The pg_upgrade --swap option makes the old cluster unusable as soon as the catalog migration process begins, necessitating a backup.

k54.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces pg_combinebackup --link, which creates hard links in the full backup pointing to the files in source backups to save disk space and time.

k55.statement: PostgreSQL 18 enables data checksums by default for new clusters.

k56.statement: MD5 password authentication is deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 in favor of SCRAM-SHA-256.

k57.statement: PostgreSQL 18 major version upgrades include statistics preservation, eliminating the need for post-upgrade ANALYZE operations.

k58.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces an asynchronous I/O framework that enables parallel execution of multiple asynchronous prefetch operations to reduce query waiting overhead.

k59.statement: PostgreSQL 18 implements Index Skip Scan, allowing multi-column B-tree indexes to be used for queries that only reference second or subsequent columns with equality constraints, reducing index reads.

k60.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces virtual generated columns, which are table columns that are dynamically calculated during query time rather than stored on disk.

k61.statement: PostgreSQL 18 supports UUIDv7, which integrates a timestamp into the high-order bits to provide time-ordered uniqueness.

k62.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces new configuration parameters (GUCs) for asynchronous I/O management, including io_method (worker, io_uring, sync) and io_max_concurrency.

k63.statement: Virtual generated columns in PostgreSQL 18 have several limitations, including no support for unique constraints, indexes, foreign keys, or logical replication.

k64.statement: Using the io_uring backend for asynchronous I/O in PostgreSQL 18 requires a relatively new Linux kernel version.

k65.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduces a new memory management system for VACUUM that reduces memory usage and improves vacuuming performance.

k66.statement: PostgreSQL 17 allows pg_upgrade to preserve logical replication slots on publishers and full subscription state on subscribers, enabling logical replication to continue after an upgrade without re-synchronization.

k67.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduces the new pg_createsubscriber utility to create logical replicas from physical standbys.

k68.statement: In PostgreSQL 17, functions used by expression indexes and materialized views that reference non-default schemas must specify a search path.

k69.statement: The feature db_user_namespace was removed in PostgreSQL 17.

k70.statement: The VACUUM process has a new internal data structure resulting in up to a 20x memory reduction and improved completion times.

k71.statement: PostgreSQL 17 supports parallel index builds for BRIN indexes.

k72.statement: PostgreSQL 17 adds support for SQL/JSON standard features including JSON_TABLE and various SQL/JSON constructor and query functions.

k73.statement: The MERGE command in PostgreSQL 17 now supports the RETURNING clause.

k74.statement: PostgreSQL 17 introduced the JSON_TABLE functionality to convert JSON data into a relational table format.

k75.statement: PostgreSQL 17 removed support for the AIX operating system.

k76.statement: PostgreSQL 17 transitioned its build system from Autotools to the Meson build system.

k77.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduced incompatibilities regarding time zone abbreviation handling, MD5 password deprecation, VACUUM/ANALYZE inheritance behavior, and COPY FROM end-of-file handling.

k78.statement: PostgreSQL 18 allows parallelized pre-upgrade checks using 'pg_upgrade --jobs' and faster directory swapping during upgrades using 'pg_upgrade --swap'.

k79.statement: Upgrading to PostgreSQL 18 requires re-running baseline benchmarks to account for new asynchronous I/O performance characteristics and potential new failure modes.

k80.statement: For PostgreSQL 18 or later, extensions must be installed into the 'Application Support' directory to ensure compatibility with Postgres.app updates.

k81.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces protocol version 3.2, which maintains backward compatibility with protocol version 3.0 (implemented in PostgreSQL 7.4 and later).

k82.statement: PostgreSQL 18 introduces the 'pgcrypto.builtin_crypto_enabled' parameter with 'on', 'off', and 'fips' settings to control built-in cryptographic function usage.

k83.statement: PostgreSQL 18 wire protocol version 3.2 is backward compatible with clients using protocol version 3.0.

k84.statement: PostgreSQL 18 server supports protocol version 3.2, but the standard client library (libpq) continues to default to protocol version 3.0.

k85.statement: The io_uring I/O method requires a Linux kernel version 5.1 or later.

k86.statement: PostgreSQL 18 must be compiled with --with-liburing support to enable the io_uring asynchronous I/O method.

k87.statement: Changing the io_method configuration parameter requires a server restart.

k88.statement: The default value for effective_io_concurrency in PostgreSQL 18 is 16, increased from 1 in PostgreSQL 17.

k89.statement: PostgreSQL 18 defaults to the 'worker' I/O method for asynchronous operations, replacing the strictly synchronous approach of PostgreSQL 17.

k90.statement: Using the 'io_uring' I/O method requires a Linux kernel version of 5.1 or newer.

k91.statement: To use the 'io_uring' I/O method, the PostgreSQL binary must be compiled with --with-liburing support.

k92.statement: High io_max_concurrency values may lead to memory pressure as async I/O consumes kernel memory for buffers and tracking.

k93.statement: The 'worker' I/O method spawns dedicated worker processes that may require increasing system process limits.

k94.statement: Users are advised to evaluate current system requirements in preparation for the PostgreSQL 18.0 release.

k95.statement: The use of IO_uring within PostgreSQL requires a modern Linux setup.
